title: Inheritance
relevance: Inheritance is core C++ OOP: interviewers probe is-a modeling, access remapping, upcasting as the base of polymorphism, and classic trivia on what is not inherited.

phases.goal: Establish what inheritance is, base vs derived, and how generalisation and specialisation organise code.

must_hit.point: Inheritance lets a new class build on an existing one, absorbing its data and behaviour while adding its own, and is how C++ models an is-a relationship.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says a derived class reuses a base and gives an is-a example such as Car is a Vehicle or Cuboid is a Rectangle.

must_hit.point: The original reused class is the base class (parent/superclass); the new inheriting class is the derived class (child/subclass).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names base/parent/superclass vs derived/child/subclass correctly.

must_hit.point: Generalisation extracts shared traits from several classes into one base; specialisation extends a general class into a more specific one that reuses the base and adds only what is unique.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts pulling Dog/Cat/Bird common behaviour into Animal versus extending Rectangle with height into Cuboid.

probes: What is inheritance in C++, and what relationship does it model?
What is the difference between generalisation and specialisation when designing a class hierarchy?

hints.1: Think about reusing an existing class versus inventing everything from scratch.
hints.2: Name the two classes in the relationship, then say whether you are extracting common behaviour upward or adding specifics downward.
hints.3: Inheritance absorbs base data and behaviour into a derived class for is-a (e.g. Car is a Vehicle); generalisation builds Animal from Dog/Cat/Bird, specialisation builds Cuboid from Rectangle.

phases.goal: Explain derivation syntax, access remapping, protected members, upcasting limits, and what is not inherited.

must_hit.point: A derived class declares the base after a colon with an access specifier, usually public, and absorbs base members so it can use them as if declared locally.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes or describes class Derived : public Base and notes inherited members like x are usable inside Derived.

must_hit.point: Inheritance mode remaps inherited member access: under public inheritance public stays public and protected stays protected; under protected inheritance public and protected become protected; under private inheritance public and protected become private; private base members stay inaccessible in all modes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks the remapping table and stresses private base members are never directly accessible regardless of mode.

must_hit.point: protected means a member is hidden from the outside world like private but remains accessible to derived classes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts outside code cannot touch protected, but a derived class member function can.

must_hit.point: Public inheritance enables safe implicit upcasting: a base pointer or reference can bind to a derived object but can only access the base portion of that object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows Animal& ref = myDog; ref.eat() works, while calling bark through the Animal interface does not.

must_hit.point: Constructors, destructors, assignment operators (operator=), and friendships are not inherited; friendship is granted explicitly and a Base friend does not automatically access Derived private members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists those four and notes base constructors still run during derived construction but are not inherited as the derived class’s own constructors.

probes: How do you write a derived class in C++, and what does the inheritance access mode do to member visibility?
What is upcasting, and what can you access through a base reference to a derived object?
What is not inherited in C++?

hints.1: Look at the colon after the derived class name and at which members you can touch from outside vs inside the hierarchy.
hints.2: Separate three ideas: how public/protected/private inheritance remaps access, that upcasting exposes only the base interface, and identity-tied members that never transfer.
hints.3: Syntax is class Derived : public Base; private base data stays inaccessible; Animal& can call eat but not bark; not inherited: constructors, destructors, operator=, friends.

phases.goal: Contrast public, protected, and private inheritance for interface exposure and is-a versus implemented-in-terms-of.

must_hit.point: Public inheritance is the standard choice: it keeps the base interface and strictly models is-a, so public members stay public and protected stay protected.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says use public inheritance when the derived type truly is a base type and clients should still see the public base API.

must_hit.point: Private inheritance makes base public and protected members private in the derived class, seals them from grandchildren, and models implemented-in-terms-of rather than is-a.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says private inheritance reuses implementation without presenting the derived type as a public base subtype.

must_hit.point: Protected inheritance makes base public and protected members protected in the derived class: inaccessible to the outside world, but a grandchild can still see them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate places protected inheritance between public and private for further derived classes versus external clients.

probes: When would you choose public inheritance versus private inheritance?
How does protected inheritance differ from private inheritance for a grandchild class?

hints.1: Ask whether clients should treat the derived object as a base object.
hints.2: Compare what happens to public base members in the derived class and whether a class derived from that derived class can still reach them.
hints.3: Public = is-a and keeps the interface; private = implemented-in-terms-of and blocks grandchildren from base members; protected hides from the world but grandchildren can still access.

phases.goal: Apply inheritance access rules and upcasting correctly in concrete class hierarchies.

must_hit.point: With public inheritance, outside code may use inherited public members on the derived object; with private inheritance those remapped members are not usable from outside.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts PublicDerived allowing pubD.pub access versus PrivateDerived rejecting external access to pub.

must_hit.point: A derived class must use the base’s public or protected functions to interact with private base data because it never has direct access to private base members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate refuses direct priv access in a derived member function and routes through base public/protected APIs.

must_hit.point: Through a base reference bound to a derived object you may call base operations, but derived-only operations are not part of the base interface.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate accepts ref.eat() on an Animal& to a Dog and rejects ref.bark() without a cast or Dog-typed handle.

probes: Given PublicDerived and PrivateDerived from the same Base, what can main() legally assign on each?
If you have Animal& ref = myDog, which calls are valid and why?

hints.1: Check the inheritance mode before deciding what outside code can see.
hints.2: For private base fields, only ask what the derived class itself can touch; for upcasting, only ask what the static base type declares.
hints.3: pubD.pub is OK under public inheritance; privD.pub is an error under private inheritance; ref.eat() works, ref.bark() does not because Animal does not know bark.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Public inheritance keeps the base interface and models is-a. Private inheritance remaps base public and protected members to private, blocks grandchildren from those members, and models implemented-in-terms-of rather than is-a.

Both hide the base from the outside world by remapping public base members away from public. Protected inheritance leaves them protected so a grandchild can still access them; private inheritance makes them private in the derived class so a grandchild cannot access any of the original base members.

Generalisation pulls shared behaviour from several classes into one base to remove duplication. Specialisation extends a general base into a more specific derived class that reuses the base design and adds only unique state or behaviour.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a derived class can directly read or write private members of its base because it inherits from it.
gotchas.correction: A derived class never has direct access to private base members under any inheritance mode; it must go through the base’s public or protected functions.

gotchas.trap: Treating a base reference or pointer to a derived object as if it exposes derived-only members.
gotchas.correction: Upcasting is safe and implicit, but the base interface only sees the base portion; derived-only calls like bark() through an Animal reference are invalid.

gotchas.trap: Believing friendships, constructors, destructors, or operator= are inherited like ordinary members.
gotchas.correction: Those are tied to class identity and are not inherited; friendship is not transitive to the derived class’s private members.

gotchas.trap: Expecting private inheritance to still behave like is-a for further derived classes or external clients.
gotchas.correction: Under private inheritance, remapped base members are private in the derived class, sealed from grandchildren, and the relationship is implemented-in-terms-of, not is-a.
